title: Per-tenant dynamic concurrency controller and jittered retry overhaul for Redis/Kafka workers
creator: Ravi Patel
description:
Background: We continue to see tail-latency spikes and periodic consumer saturations for high-throughput tenants. Root causes we've observed: (1) static per-worker concurrency caps that don't respect tenant-level traffic patterns, (2) synchronized retry bursts across workers causing temporary overload, and (3) limited signal surface in the current lease/semaphore model to make fast shedding decisions.

Goal: Replace the global/static concurrency control with a per-tenant dynamic concurrency controller that adapts to real-time latency, error rate, and queue depth signals and pair it with an overhaul of retry semantics using exponential backoff + full jitter and per-tenant retry state to avoid synchronized retry storms. We aim for lower 95/99th token latencies, fewer transient 5xx error cascades, and more graceful degradation during capacity constraints.

Design overview:
- Concurrency controller: implement a controller that maintains a token-bucket-style concurrency allowance per tenant. The controller adjusts tokens/sec and max-burst based on a rolling window of metrics: median/95/99 latency, error ratio, and inflight queue length. Controllers run in-process per worker but fetch tenant-tier config from the control plane and emit metrics to Console.
- Slow-path detection: when error rate or 99th latency crosses thresholds, the controller will proactively reduce allowed concurrency for that tenant and increase retry backoff multipliers. Reduction uses multiplicative backoff with a cooldown period to avoid flapping.
- Retry redesign: move from fixed retry counts + fixed delays to configurable exponential backoff with full jitter (per-tenant base/backoff cap) and algorithmic pacing that respects controller token availability. Retries are treated as lower priority (lower weight) when tokens are scarce.
- Leaseless soft-eviction: remove reliance on a global worker lease for backpressure decisions. Instead use local lease-less heuristics combined with a lightweight distributed grace flag in Redis (small per-tenant state key) to coordinate shedding across workers in a best-effort fashion without strict locks.
- Integration with Kafka consumers: for Kafka-driven pipelines, the concurrency controller will annotate offsets with in-flight tokens and use cooperative pausing (consumer.pause()/resume()) when tenant tokens are exhausted to avoid polling hot partitions.
- Observability and SLOs: add per-tenant metrics (allowed_tokens, used_tokens, retry_rate, retry_latency, controller_actions) and Console dashboards. Wire regression alerts for >10% increase in 99th latency or >5% increase in retry_rate.

Migration plan:
1) Feature flag the controller and retry behavior per-cluster and per-tenant. Start with internal and low-volume tenants.
2) Roll out read-only metrics only to validate signals and thresholds for 1 week.
3) Enable soft-shedding heuristics and staggered concurrency reductions for an initial cohort of 5 tenants.
4) Scale up to 30% of traffic, monitor, then enable for all tenants by default, with opt-out per tenant.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for token accounting and backoff math.
- Integration tests simulating tenant bursts, worker restarts, and Redis/Kafka failovers.
- Chaos test: inject increased latency on model endpoints and ensure controller reduces concurrency and that retries spread over time rather than forming a spike.
- Load test: synthetic tenants to validate stable throughput and reduced tail latency.

Rollback and fallback paths:
- Feature flag to revert to static concurrency and previous retry behavior.
- Kill-switch in the control plane to set all per-tenant tokens to previous global caps.

Success criteria:
- 20% reduction in end-to-end 99th latency for affected tenants in load tests.
- 50% reduction in synchronized retry bursts measured as second-over-second retry spikes.
- No increase in error surface area for non-target tenants.

Notes:
- This ticket intentionally avoids a heavy distributed locking scheme to reduce operational fragility; we rely on eventual consistency for shedding coordination.
- Security review not required unless we start storing customer-configured backoff parameters in plaintext in control plane configs.
